names.official: Income tax (PAYE and self-assessment, with the withholding taxes on dividends, professional services and non-resident landlords)

taxes.base: Income of individuals from employment, business, rents, investments and other sources; PAYE is deducted by employers each pay day.
taxes.payer: Individuals; employers deduct PAYE and self-employed people file a return.

rate.headline: 20% and 40% with tax credits
details: A single person pays 20% on the first EUR 44,000 of taxable income in 2025 and 40% above, less personal and earned-income credits.
Withholding taxes on dividends, on payments for professional services and to non-resident landlords are folded into the line.

instruments.explanation: The second largest tax in 2025, after corporation tax. PAYE (EUR 25.8 billion) is about 85% of the line; the Universal Social Charge is a separate tax and is drawn apart.

taxes.base: Gross income of individuals above a small threshold, with no allowance for reliefs.
taxes.payer: Individuals; employers deduct it with PAYE.

rate.headline: 0.5% to 8%
details: 2025 rates: 0.5% on the first EUR 12,012, 2% up to EUR 28,700, 3% up to EUR 70,044 and 8% above.
Self-employed people with non-PAYE income over EUR 100,000 pay a further 3%.

instruments.explanation: A separate charge on top of income tax, introduced in 2011 to replace two earlier levies. Its name suggests social insurance, but it is a tax paid into the general Exchequer.

taxes.base: Interest paid on deposits by banks and other deposit takers.
taxes.payer: Depositors; the bank deducts it.

instruments.explanation: Revenue rose by 44% in 2025 as deposit rates were higher.

names.official: Exit tax on life assurance policies and investment funds

taxes.base: Gains on life assurance policies and on investment funds, taxed on payments and on each eighth anniversary.
taxes.payer: The insurer or fund manager, on behalf of the investor.

rate.headline: A flat rate on the gain
details: The rate is set by the Act and applies to both policies and funds.

instruments.explanation: Taxes the return on pooled savings in place of income tax and capital gains tax.

taxes.base: Profits of companies resident in Ireland and of branches of foreign companies.
taxes.payer: Companies.

rate.headline: 12.5% trading, 25% passive, 15% for large groups
details: 12.5% on trading income and 25% on non-trading income.
Groups with revenues of EUR 750 million or more pay a minimum of 15% under the global minimum tax rules.

instruments.explanation: Receipts of EUR 34.7 billion in 2025 include about EUR 1.8 billion of one-off money after the EU court ruling on Apple; underlying receipts were EUR 32.9 billion, and a small number of multinational groups pay a large part of them.

taxes.base: Supplies of goods and services in Ireland and imports, with credit for tax paid on business purchases.
taxes.payer: Consumers; businesses charge it and remit the balance.

rate.headline: 23% standard, 13.5% and 9% reduced
details: Most food, children’s clothing and books are zero-rated.
Imports are charged at the border and appear in the same line.

instruments.explanation: About a fifth of net receipts in a year of high corporation tax. VAT collected on sales to other EU countries through the one-stop shop (EUR 13.4 billion) belongs to those states and is not counted.

taxes.base: Instruments that transfer property, shares and other assets, and some insurance policies.
taxes.payer: The buyer or the person named in the instrument.

rate.headline: Residential 1%–2%, shares 1%, non-residential 7.5%
details: Residential property: 1% up to EUR 1 million and 2% above.
Shares: 1%. Non-residential property: 7.5%.

instruments.explanation: One tax in law, three lines in the Revenue figures: property (EUR 821 million), shares (540) and other instruments (536).

taxes.base: Gains on the disposal of assets such as shares, land and business interests.
taxes.payer: The person who sells.

details: Reliefs apply to retirement relief and to disposals of the principal private residence.

instruments.explanation: Receipts rose by about a quarter in 2025.

names.official: Capital acquisitions tax (gift and inheritance tax)

taxes.base: Gifts and inheritances received over a lifetime, above a threshold that depends on the relationship to the giver.
taxes.payer: The person who receives the gift or inheritance.

rate.headline: 33% above the threshold
details: The lifetime threshold for a child receiving from a parent (group A) is EUR 400,000 from October 2024.

instruments.explanation: Receipts rose by almost a third in 2025.

taxes.base: Goods imported from outside the European Union, at the common external tariff.
taxes.payer: Importers.

rate.headline: EU common external tariff
details: Rates are set by the European Union for all member states.

instruments.explanation: Revenue collects the duty for the EU. It reports duty collected of EUR 616 million but does not say how much is passed to the EU budget.

taxes.base: Petrol, auto diesel, marked gas oil and other mineral oils, per litre, at the point of release from an excise warehouse.
taxes.payer: Fuel suppliers; passed on at the pump.

rate.headline: Per litre, temporarily reduced in 2026
details: The Government cut the rates on auto fuels in 2026 and deferred the carbon tax increase to 14 October 2026; the Department of Finance estimates the cost at about EUR 432 million.

instruments.explanation: Light oils (petrol) yielded EUR 613 million in 2025 and heavy oils (mostly diesel) EUR 1,476 million.

taxes.base: The carbon content of mineral oils, solid fuels and natural gas.
taxes.payer: Suppliers of the fuels; passed on to consumers.

rate.headline: EUR 71 per tonne of CO2 (from 8 October 2025)
details: The rate rose from EUR 63.50 on 8 October 2025.

instruments.explanation: Introduced in 2009 and raised every year; receipts more than doubled between 2020 and 2025.

taxes.base: The open-market selling price of a vehicle at first registration in Ireland.
taxes.payer: The person who registers the vehicle.

rate.headline: A percentage of the price, by CO2 band
details: Rates rise with the vehicle’s emissions; electric vehicles pay the lowest band.

instruments.explanation: Tied to new and imported car sales.

taxes.base: The annual licence to keep a vehicle on the road, by CO2 emissions for cars and by engine size or weight for others.
taxes.payer: Vehicle owners.

rate.headline: A fixed annual amount by CO2 band or engine size

instruments.explanation: A national tax whose proceeds go to the Local Government Fund.

taxes.base: Beer, wine, spirits and cider, by volume of alcohol or product.
taxes.payer: Producers and importers; passed on in the price.

rate.headline: Per litre of pure alcohol or per product
details: Wine yielded EUR 402 million in 2025, beer 394, spirits 392 and cider 48.

instruments.explanation: Revenue is split almost equally between wine, beer and spirits.

taxes.base: Cigarettes and other tobacco products.
taxes.payer: Manufacturers and importers; passed on in the price.

rate.headline: A specific amount per cigarette plus a share of the price

instruments.explanation: Revenue rose from EUR 976 million in 2024 to EUR 1,009 million in 2025.

names.official: Betting duty, sugar-sweetened drinks tax, e-liquid products tax and electricity tax

taxes.base: Bets placed with bookmakers, sugar-sweetened drinks, e-liquids for vapes and electricity supplied.
taxes.payer: Bookmakers, producers and importers, electricity suppliers.

rate.headline: By product
details: Each tax has its own base and rate in its Act.

instruments.explanation: Four small excise taxes grouped because each is below 0.1% of the national total: betting duty EUR 113.7 million, sugar-sweetened drinks tax 30.5, e-liquid tax 5.6 and electricity tax 5.2.

taxes.base: Earnings of employees and the income of self-employed people, by insurance class.
taxes.payer: Employees, employers and the self-employed.

rate.headline: A share of earnings, by class
details: The Social Welfare (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2024 raises the rates by 0.1 percentage point each October from 2024 to 2028.

instruments.explanation: Pays for the State pension, jobseeker’s and maternity benefits through the Social Insurance Fund. Revenue collects it with PAYE.

taxes.base: The self-assessed market value of residential property, revalued every few years.
taxes.payer: Owners of residential property.

rate.headline: About 0.1% of the value, higher on very valuable homes
details: Councils may raise or lower the basic rate by up to 15%.
Revenue pays the proceeds into the Local Government Fund, which funds councils; the Exchequer adds equalisation money.

instruments.explanation: Collected by Revenue, spent by councils, and the only recurring tax on homes in Ireland.

taxes.base: The valuation of commercial and industrial premises, set by Tailte Éireann.
taxes.payer: Occupiers of business premises.

rate.headline: An annual rate on valuation set by each council
details: Each council sets its annual rate on valuation in its budget; for 2025 Mayo set 0.247 and Sligo 0.2536.

instruments.explanation: The largest single income stream of local authorities, about a quarter of their funding on average.
